extracted.intended_audience: general readers of travel literature; prospective travellers and diplomats
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century travelogue chapter describing the Persian court, its ceremonies, personalities, and reflections on manners, reform, and the ethics of travel writing. Contains both narrative reportage and explicit authorial guidance about how to write and think about foreign societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit personal narrative to observed facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "all these exciting subjects are forbidden me, by a stupid rule I have laid down, which compels me, in all that I personally relate, to limit myself to facts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial rule: do not invent sensational scenes or fabricate intrigues when relating personal experiences. Anti-pattern: creating imagined seraglio scenes (Circassians, intrigues, murders) to titillate readers. Example guidance in text: the author explicitly declines to 'paint Circassians... devise well-planned intrigues, hair-breadth escapes, and hint at murders' and instead promises to stick to facts. Use direct observation or credible testimony rather than fiction when presenting 'personal' accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach foreign peoples with humility and indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: "May he find enough of sound and good feeling among its inhabitants to make him look with indulgence on their failings and excesses... may he contemplate it in a spirit of humility, which rather leads him to question the correctness of his own judgment, than to pronounce, on a superficial glance, that every thing is wrong..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance for travellers and writers: emphasize the positive and admirable aspects of the society you visit; avoid quick, superficial condemnation based on differences of religion, language, or custom. Anti-patterns: treating other societies as wholly 'wrong' because they differ from one's own habits; prideful, superior attitudes. Recommendation: cultivate tolerance and question your own judgments before passing harsh verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer slow, context-aware reform over rapid transplantation of foreign institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: "My plans of slow and almost imperceptible change... have been ridiculed... A medicine may be excellent in itself, yet, from the peculiar habits and constitution of the patient, it may act as a poison."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising political or social reform (as a traveller, advisor, or diplomat), consider local conditions, customs, and capacities; favour gradual, inclusive approaches rather than sudden wholesale importation of foreign systems. Anti-patterns: assuming that institutions effective at home will automatically benefit another country; advocating rapid 'regeneration' without accounting for societal readiness. Use cautious, evidence-based proposals and small pilot efforts (the author suggests confined experiments such as limited road-making) to test reforms before wider implementation.
